exam: What immediate steps do you take for a woman at 33 weeks with regular contractions and cervical dilation of 2 cm? — Assess fetal wellbeing, give steroids, start nifedipine, rule out infection, arrange transfer if needed.
How would you differentiate true preterm labour from false labour in a low‑resource setting? — Look for regularity, duration, cervical change, and use bedside doppler for fetal heart pattern.
Why is nifedipine preferred over magnesium sulfate for tocolysis in most cases? — It is effective, has fewer maternal side‑effects, and does not cause respiratory depression.

A patient with HIV on ART presents with PTL. Which infection should you screen for and why? — Screen for urinary tract infection and bacterial vaginosis, as they are common precipitants and may be asymptomatic.
Explain the role of antenatal corticosteroids and the timing of their administration. — They accelerate fetal lung surfactant production; give two doses 24 h apart, ideally 48 h before delivery.
What are the red‑flag signs that mandate urgent delivery regardless of gestational age? — Massive hemorrhage, uterine rupture, severe maternal sepsis, non‑reassuring fetal heart rate.
When is progesterone prophylaxis indicated and how is it administered? — In women with prior PTL or a short cervix, given as daily vaginal micronized progesterone.
How does a bicornuate uterus increase the risk of preterm labour? — Abnormal uterine shape limits space, leading to early cervical change and inefficient uterine contractility.
ai.title: Preterm Labour
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Preterm labour is uterine activity leading to cervical change before 37 weeks. Recognise risk factors, diagnose with history, exam and simple tests, and act promptly to delay delivery and treat underlying causes.

b: Contractions: ≥5 in 10 min, lasting ≥30 s, confirmed by palpation or bedside doppler.
Cervical change: dilation ≥2 cm or effacement ≥80 % on vaginal exam.
sections.p: Preterm labour is regular uterine contractions causing cervical effacement or dilation before 37 weeks gestation. Diagnosis requires at least two of: documented contractions, cervical change, and gestational age <37 weeks.

b: Stage guides urgency of tocolysis and transfer.
sections.p: Stage I: Contractions with cervical length ≥25 mm on trans‑vaginal ultrasound. Stage II: Cervical length 10‑24 mm, no dilation. Stage III: Dilation ≥2 cm or ruptured membranes.

b: Infection: urinary tract infection, bacterial vaginosis, group B streptococcus, malaria, HIV‑related opportunistic infections.
Uterine anomaly: bicornuate or septate uterus.
Previous obstetric history: prior PTL, pre‑eclampsia, caesarean scar.
Maternal stress, smoking, low socioeconomic status.
sections.p: Identify precipitating factors; in low‑resource settings infections and uterine anomalies dominate.

b: Pain often lower abdomen, radiating to back.
Bleeding: usually spotting, may indicate placental issues.
Fluid: clear amniotic fluid suggests membrane rupture.
sections.p: A pregnant woman reports regular painful uterine tightening, sometimes with vaginal bleeding or fluid loss. On exam, she has a tender uterus, cervical change, and may have a low‑grade fever if infection is present.

t.b: Is there a high risk of delivery within 7 days? Positive predicts increased risk; negative has high NPV, allowing safe expectant management.
What is the risk of imminent PTL? Length <25 mm indicates higher risk; >25 mm suggests lower risk.
Is there a urinary infection? Positive nitrites/leukocyte esterase prompts antibiotics; culture guides choice.

t.a: Vaginal swab for bacterial vaginosis / GBS
t.b: Is there pathogenic flora? Treat with appropriate antibiotics to reduce PTL risk.

t.b: Is there risk of allo‑immunisation? Important for planning delivery and neonatal care.

t.b: What is cervical status? Provides crude staging when imaging not possible.

b: Maternal sepsis, uterine rupture, placental abruption.
Fetal distress: abnormal heart rate, reduced movements.
sections.p: Rapid cervical change, heavy bleeding, severe abdominal pain, or signs of infection demand urgent transfer.

b: Antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone) for fetal lung maturity – give even if delivery may be imminent.
Tocolytics: nifedipine (first line) or atosiban where available; avoid magnesium sulfate unless for neuroprotection or pre‑eclampsia.
Antibiotics for proven infection (e.g., ampicillin‑gentamicin for urinary infection, metronidazole for bacterial vaginosis).
Treat underlying anemia, correct electrolytes, give fluids judiciously.
If membranes ruptured, give prophylactic antibiotics and consider delivery if >34 weeks or infection worsens.
sections.p: Goal: delay delivery ≥48 h to allow antenatal steroids and transfer if needed, while treating the underlying cause.

b: Schedule antenatal visits every 2 weeks until 28 weeks, then weekly.
Educate on signs of recurrent labour.
sections.p: After acute episode, monitor cervical length weekly, counsel on smoking cessation, treat asymptomatic bacteriuria, and provide progesterone (vaginal micronized) for high‑risk women.

b: False labour: irregular, non‑progressive contractions, no cervical change.
Pre‑eclampsia: hypertension, proteinuria, edema; labour pain may be present but accompanied by systemic signs.
sections.p: Distinguish from false labour (Braxton‑Hicks), uterine irritability, and pre‑eclampsia‑related uterine pain.

b: Rely on combination of clinical exam and imaging, not a single test.
sections.p: A negative fFN does not rule out labour if cervical length is already short; infection may be missed if only urine dipstick is used.
